set.n: Forty casks of beer under the old Henderson brewery (located 1925, not known raised)
set.st: Brewer Joseph Ritter stored forty barrels of beer in a cellar dug 30 ft into a hillside about the 1860s; the tunnel caved in. Owner Charles Ney razed the brewery in summer 1925, and in Oct 1925 the UP reported two huge oak casks buried about 60 years earlier in the hillside tunnel. By 7 Nov 1925 the beer was in dispute: the county attorney said it was wet contraband and could not be moved, an heir of Ritter in St Paul claimed a share, and Ney's son said his father would take no further steps to take possession until the legal problems were settled (Ney would sell to anyone who wanted to go into 'beer mining'). In May 1926 four young men sank a shaft 30 ft down with Ney's permission and a chart from old brewery employees; a digging party at 'the ruins of the old Ritter brewery' was halted by heavy masonry, and old-timers doubted the casks were there. On 23 May 1926 five Henderson men (Mimbach, Whelan, Teschendorf, Beecher and Hensler) said the dig had stalled, that it might take a steam shovel and dynamite, and that they were looking for a backer. No recovery is reported in print through 1928.
set.t: Casks located in 1925 but never reported raised; look-only. The 1894 Sanborn map (sheet 1) shows the Jno. Enes Brewery about 1/2 mile south of the post office, built against the hill beside the road up the bluff, with ice houses and a malt house; it is the only brewery on the 1894 and 1910 Sanborns, so the pin is on it; that it was Ritter's earlier plant is an inference. In 1926 the site was called the old Ritter brewery ruins; whether it is the 'Jno. Enes Brewery' of the 1894 Sanborn is unconfirmed (Enes may have been Ritter's successor). The 1880 census confirms an Enes brewery: John Enes, 53, and Christian Enes, 25, brewers, alongside Joseph Ritter, 52, and Albert Miller, 27, also brewers, so Henderson had two brewing families.
set.tovw: Casks located 1925 in the caved tunnel; 1926 dig stalled; no recovery found in print through 1928
set.y: stored c.1865; tunnel found Oct-Nov 1925; dig May 1926 stalled

set.st: Herman Rechenberg spent four years spading his late father's farm. In January 1924, digging sand in the cellar for his chickens, he struck a glass jar holding about $1,300 in mildewed bills, which he banked at the Produce Exchange Bank, St Paul. He found it on Thursday 17 January 1924: $1,360 in mildewed bills. His father, 48 years on the homestead from about 1864, had died about 1912 apparently without money even for his burial. The 1910 and 1920 censuses put Anton and Herman Rechenberg in Mendota Twp (today's Mendota Heights), not West St Paul; the 1916 Dakota atlas shows no Rechenberg on the Mendota plate, so the parcel awaits the 1928 plat. In May 1924 a jury trial at Hastings heard who had buried the jar: sister Bertha said she buried it herself, and sister Emma claimed a third; Judge Albert Johnson of the Dakota Co District Court ordered the three to share equally.
set.n: Rechenberg's jar of mildewed bills, Dodd Road farm, Mendota Heights ($1,360, found 1924, divided by court)
set.pl: Farm 'near Mendota', Dodd Road area; parcel not found (1916 atlas hatched city)
set.tovw: Recovered Jan 1924 ($1,360); divided by court May 1924
